prompt: A nightly backup job has reported success every night for a year. What has that established?
hint: What does an exit code describe: the program, or what it left behind?

choices.text: That last night's copy can rebuild the database
choices.why: Only a restore establishes that. The job's status is a statement about the job.

choices.text: That a program ran each night and did not report an error
choices.why: Right. Whether the bytes it left can become a database again is a separate question, answered by restoring them.

choices.text: That every copy is complete, because a partial dump exits with an error
choices.why: A dump of the wrong database is complete, exits cleanly and is useless. Completeness of the wrong thing is not a backup.

choices.text: That the copies are stored somewhere the database cannot take with it
choices.why: The job knows nothing about where its output ends up living, or what else lives there.

prompt: In 2017 GitLab had five ways to get its production database back, and none worked as intended. What would have found every one of those failures in advance?
hint: Some of the five had never been set up for that server at all.

choices.text: Alerting on the exit code of every backup job
choices.why: The failing dump's reports were being sent and rejected, and two of the mechanisms had no job to alert on: they had never been configured.

choices.text: Keeping more copies of each kind of backup, in more places
choices.why: More copies of a dump that fails, or of a snapshot nobody enabled, are more of nothing.

choices.text: Restoring from each of them recently and checking the result
choices.why: Right. A restore exercises every link at once, including the ones nobody remembered existed.

choices.text: Snapshotting by hand more often
choices.why: That snapshot is what saved them. It was taken for another reason, and it is not what was broken.

prompt: Which of these failures would a backup job's exit code never reveal? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask of each one whether any program in the job sees it go wrong.

choices.text: The job dumps a database that still exists but is no longer the one in use
choices.why: Right. Every program succeeds; the copy is complete and of the wrong thing.

choices.text: pg_dump, run on its own in the job, cannot connect to the server
choices.why: On its own, with nothing after it in a pipe, pg_dump exits with an error and the job sees it.

choices.text: The copies are written to the same disk as the database
choices.why: Right. Writing to that disk succeeds every night, until the disk fails and takes both.

choices.text: Restoring takes longer than the business is willing to wait
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the backup job measures how long the reverse journey takes.

prompt: A team restores its backup into a test server every quarter and checks it with a report. The database has to be back within two hours of a disaster, and the last drill took nine. Which describes them?
hint: Two different things can work or fail: the copy, and the recovery.

choices.text: Their backups have failed the drill
choices.why: The drill restored the data and the report matched, so the copies are good. What failed is the time.

choices.text: Their backups work and their recovery does not
choices.why: Right. A copy that comes back too slowly to matter is a working backup and a failed recovery. Lesson 8 makes the two hours a number somebody signs.

choices.text: They are covered, because the drill restored the data and checked it
choices.why: Seven hours past the agreed limit is not covered: the business waits nine hours either way.

choices.text: They need to take backups more often
choices.why: More frequent copies reduce how much data is lost, not how long the restore takes.

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine rather than installing PostgreSQL on the computer you work on?
hint: Think about what the course asks you to do to the server.

choices.text: PostgreSQL does not run on Windows or macOS
choices.why: It runs on both. The recommendation is about what you do to it, not whether it runs.

choices.text: The platform connects to it to check your exercises
choices.why: The platform runs nothing on your machine and connects to nothing. The lab is entirely yours.

choices.text: You will break it on purpose, and that has to cost nothing
choices.why: Right. Throwing a virtual machine away costs nothing, and a snapshot puts it back in seconds.

choices.text: It runs faster than an installed server
choices.why: If anything it is a little slower. Speed is not the reason.

prompt: A student plans to take this course against a managed PostgreSQL service from a cloud provider. What would they be missing?
hint: What does a managed service keep to itself?

choices.text: A client that can connect and run queries
choices.why: Every managed service accepts psql. Querying is the part it does give you.

choices.text: Room for a database the size of the shop
choices.why: The shop is half a megabyte compressed; any service holds it.

choices.text: The ability to run pg_dump against it from your own computer
choices.why: pg_dump is an ordinary client and works against managed services. It is the server side that is missing.

choices.text: Its files, its replication and the right to kill it
choices.why: Right. Those are what the course is about, and a managed service keeps all three. Lesson 21 is the lesson you could take there.

prompt: The course runs several PostgreSQL servers on one machine. Which failure can this lab only simulate?
hint: What do servers on one computer share?

choices.text: A cable cut between the primary and its standby
choices.why: Right. Servers on one machine share a network card, so a cut is simulated by blocking a port, and the lessons say so when they do it.

choices.text: A primary that crashes halfway through writing a transaction
choices.why: Killing the process does exactly that, for real.

choices.text: A table dropped by mistake in the middle of the afternoon
choices.why: That is as real on one machine as on fifty: one statement.

choices.text: A replica that falls behind its primary
choices.why: Lag is real here; lesson 13 produces it and measures it.

prompt: How many rows does `shop.sql` put in the `orders` table?
hint: The second generate_series.

prompt: Why does `shop.sql` compute customers and totals with a multiplication and a remainder rather than with `random()`?
hint: What do later lessons compare the restored shop against?

choices.text: Because random() would be too slow on fifty thousand rows
choices.why: It would take well under a second. Speed is not what the choice protects.

choices.text: So every run produces the same rows, anywhere
choices.why: Right. A restored shop is compared against counts and sums the lessons print, and those only mean something if your shop and the recorded one are identical.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL has no random number function
choices.why: It has random(). The script avoids it on purpose.

choices.text: So that the totals look like real prices from a real shop
choices.why: They look like nothing in particular. They are scattered, and repeatable.

prompt: Of the columns `pg_lsclusters` prints, the course returns most to the data directory and the ___, which is the first place to look when a server refuses to start.
hint: The right-hand column.

prompt: `pg_restore -d shop_restored shop.dump` printed nothing at all. What does that tell you about `shop_restored`?
hint: Compare it with what a nightly job's green tick tells you.

choices.text: That shop_restored is identical to shop, row for row
choices.why: Identical is what the report establishes. pg_restore only said it met no error.

choices.text: That pg_restore met no error, and nothing more
choices.why: Right. Silence is the same evidence as a green job, which is why the report exists.

choices.text: That nothing was restored, since a restore prints each table
choices.why: pg_restore is quiet when it succeeds. Silence is not emptiness.

choices.text: That the restore carries on in the background
choices.why: pg_restore returns when it has finished; nothing runs on afterwards.

prompt: Why does every query in `verify.sql` end in an ORDER BY or return a single row?
hint: What would diff see if two identical databases returned rows in different orders?

choices.text: Because diff needs sorted input before it will compare two files
choices.why: diff compares line by line in whatever order it is given. Sorted input is not a requirement.

choices.text: So that the largest tables are compared first
choices.why: The order is about rows within a query, not which table comes first.

choices.text: Two identical copies could print rows in different orders
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL may return unordered rows in any order, and a drill that fails on that is a drill nobody trusts.

choices.text: So that the report runs faster on large tables
choices.why: Sorting costs time; it is there for correctness, not speed.

prompt: In a restored copy, one order in the middle of the table has its total changed from 1500 to 1510 cents, and nothing else differs. Which lines of the report change?
hint: Which queries read total_cents?

choices.text: The orders line's count
choices.why: The number of orders is the same: no row was added or removed.

choices.text: The indexes line
choices.why: A changed value does not add or remove an index.

choices.text: None: the report counts rows and cannot see a changed value
choices.why: It sums total_cents precisely so that it can see one.

choices.text: The orders sum, and the sum for that customer's city
choices.why: Right. Both sums read total_cents, so both move by ten. The counts and max(id) stay put.

prompt: After one order was deleted from `shop_restored`, the report's orders line read `49999|50000|524979229` against the live `50000|50000|524985000`. What was the deleted order's total, in cents?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: What does `-X` do in `psql -X -A -t shop -f verify.sql`?
hint: The report should not depend on who runs it.

choices.text: It skips your personal ~/.psqlrc settings
choices.why: Right. A ~/.psqlrc that prints NULL differently, or turns on timing, would make two people's reports differ for the same data, so -X leaves it out.

choices.text: It prints values separated by a bar, with no padding
choices.why: That is -A, the unaligned output.

choices.text: It runs the whole file inside one transaction
choices.why: That is -1, or --single-transaction.

choices.text: It leaves out the column headers and the row count
choices.why: That is -t, tuples only.

prompt: `pg_dump shpo | gzip > shop.sql.gz` failed to find the database, and `echo $?` printed 0. Why?
hint: Whose exit status does a pipeline report?

choices.text: pg_dump exits with 0 when the database does not exist
choices.why: It exits with an error; that status is simply not the one the shell reports.

choices.text: gzip swallowed pg_dump's error message along with its output
choices.why: The message reached the screen. It is the status that was lost, not the text.

choices.text: A pipeline reports its last program's status, and gzip succeeded
choices.why: Right. gzip compressed what it was given, which was nothing, and did it perfectly.

choices.text: The shell ignores errors written to the terminal
choices.why: No such rule. The shell reports the last program's status, and pg_dump was not the last.

prompt: How many bytes was the `shop.sql.gz` that the failed pipeline left behind?
hint: ls -l printed it.

prompt: A backup script starts with `set -euo pipefail`. Which failure does it still report as success?
hint: pipefail catches programs that fail. Which of these involves no failing program?

choices.text: pg_dump cannot connect to the server
choices.why: pg_dump exits with an error, pipefail passes it on, and set -e stops the script.

choices.text: The disk fills up while gzip is writing
choices.why: gzip fails to write and exits with an error, which the job now sees.

choices.text: pg_dump copies a database the application stopped using
choices.why: Right. Every program succeeds. Only a restore, checked against what the real data answers, notices.

choices.text: The out-of-memory killer stops pg_dump
choices.why: A killed process exits with a failing status, and pipefail reports it.

prompt: Put the three checks every backup job in this course ends with in order, cheapest first.
hint: One of them needs a second server.
items: Every program in the job succeeded
The output exists and is not much smaller than the last one
The copy has been restored somewhere and checked
trap: Exit codes cost nothing to read; a size comparison costs a file listing; a restore costs a server and time, and is the only one that proves the copy.

prompt: Match each message with what it means.
hint: Read the part after FATAL.

pairs.right: The server runs and has no role with your name
You are known, and asked for a database nobody created
You are not the computer's postgres user
No server is listening on the socket

right_distractors: The password you typed was wrong

prompt: `pg_lsclusters` says the main cluster is down, and `sudo pg_ctlcluster 16 main start` fails. Where is the reason?
hint: pg_lsclusters names a file for each cluster.

choices.text: In the log named in pg_lsclusters' last column
choices.why: Right. The server writes why it refused to start, a full disk or a bad setting, to that log.

choices.text: In the message psql printed when it could not connect
choices.why: psql only knows nothing answered. Why the server is not there is in the server's own log.

choices.text: In the ~/.psqlrc file psql reads every time it starts
choices.why: That file configures your psql client; it cannot stop a server starting.

choices.text: In the output of createuser
choices.why: createuser talks to a running server. With none running, it has nothing to say about why.

prompt: A colleague proposes checking backups by alerting when a night's file is more than 10% smaller than the previous night's. Which failure would that check never catch?
hint: Which failure produces a file of a steady, normal size?

choices.text: A typo that leaves a twenty-byte file
choices.why: Twenty bytes against half a megabyte is a drop of nearly 100%; the alert fires the first night.

choices.text: A steady-sized dump of the wrong database
choices.why: Right. A steady size is exactly what the check expects, so a steady wrong copy passes it every night.

choices.text: A dump cut short halfway because the disk filled
choices.why: Half the size is a 50% drop, well past the threshold.

choices.text: A dump that stops after the first of two tables
choices.why: Losing the bigger table shrinks the file far past 10%.

prompt: You join a team whose database is backed up nightly. The backups have never been restored. What is the first useful thing to do?
hint: Which single action tests every link of the chain?

choices.text: Add set -o pipefail to the top of the backup script
choices.why: Worth doing, and it only catches failing programs. It says nothing about whether last night's copy restores.

choices.text: Restore last night's copy elsewhere and compare it
choices.why: Right. Until that happens, nobody knows whether the team has a backup at all.

choices.text: Increase how often the job runs
choices.why: More copies of something never restored are more unknowns.

choices.text: Move the copies to a different disk
choices.why: Also worth doing later. First find out whether what you would be moving is a backup.
